newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil probes manipulation behind plunge-report.
newsitem.headline: Brazil probes manipulation behind plunge-report.

text.p: The Brazilian government suspects manipulation by large banks may have played a part in this week's rollercoaster ride on the Sao Paulo bolsa, which plunged 4.7 percent on Friday, newspapers reported on Saturday.

The Jornal do Brasil and Correio Braziliense dailies said the Securities Exchange Commission (CVM) suspected some major players wanted stock prices to drop because otherwise they stood to lose millions of dollars in the futures market.

"There are today many small and medium size investors who we cannot allow to be hurt by the actions of manipulators," CVM head Francisco Costa e Silva told Jornal do Brasil economic columnist Guilherme Barros.
"It's important that these small investors be protected and so we are going to analyse everything that happened these last days," Costa e Silva said.
Brazilian shares have spent the past week rising and sinking sharply amid nervousness after Thailand and the Philippines were forced into de facto currency devaluations.

Economists say Brazil has many of the characterictics that made those countries and other emerging markets vulnerable to speculative attacks, such as widening current account and trade gaps, an overvalued currency and loose fiscal controls.

Even though Brazil's fundamentals are generally acknowledged to be more solid, investors used the currency woes in Asia as a pretext to dump Brazilian shares, which had soared an extraordinary 80 percent since the beginning of the year.
Correio Braziliense, also quoting Costa e Silva, said several large banks stood to lose millions of dollars if the bull run went on unhindered.

It said they had betted in the futures market on the market coming down. The Asian foreign exchange crisis gave the banks the excuse they needed to force share prices lower in a concerted selling campaign.
The newspapers said Costa e Silva declined to name the banks he suspected of involvement in the operation.
Traders and analysts found it difficult to explain Friday's share plunge, which reversed gains made the previous day.

They said many small-time investors, the doctors and dentists who fuelled the Bovespa's surge in the first half of 1997, had gotten cold feet after the week's oscillations and had decided to take their profits and run.
